91.quote_or_event: “Her speech is sweet, and her way of life is humble. She enjoys the Bed of her Husband Lord.”
91.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the soul-bride who has found her Husband Lord through the Guru: her inner union shows outwardly as sweet speech and humble conduct.
91.tie_back: As Valluvar says truly sweet words come from those who have grasped what is right, Gurbani treats sweet speech as the fruit of a soul that has found the Truth.
91.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 31, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
91._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on sweet speech flowing from inner realization; the verse does not separately name freedom from guile, and its bride image is spiritual, not romantic.

92.quote_or_event: “He speaks sweetly, moves humbly and giving away something by his hands for the well being of others feels happy.”
92.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh exegete, lists sweet speech, humble conduct and giving with one's own hands as the marks of the Guru's Sikh.
92.tie_back: It sets kind speech beside generous giving, the very two goods the Kural compares, though without ranking one above the other.
92.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 28, Pauri 15 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)
92._accuracy_note: Partial: pairs sweet speech with giving but does not rank the cheerful face and kind word above the gift; Bhai Gurdas is authoritative early exegesis, not scripture. Wording verified via the BaniDB database behind searchgurbani.

93.quote_or_event: “My Dear Lord and Master, my Friend, speaks so sweetly. I have grown weary of testing Him, but still, He never speaks harshly to me.”
93.explanation: Guru Arjan describes God himself as a Friend whose speech is unfailingly sweet, making gentle speech an attribute of the divine.
93.tie_back: If sweetness of word is the Lord's own character, then, as the Kural says, a kind word from the heart is itself virtue rather than a mere means to it.
93.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
93._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse praises God's sweet speech rather than defining human virtue, and it omits the Kural's welcoming face and kindly look.

94.quote_or_event: “A mild spoken, humble and giver through his hands moves in equipoise and remains happy.”
94.explanation: Bhai Gurdas holds that the person who speaks gently, walks humbly and gives freely lives in calm contentment.
94.tie_back: Like the Kural's promise that those who speak gladdening words to all will escape misery, it ties mild speech to a life free of distress.
94.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 12, Pauri 16 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)
94._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on gentle speech yielding happiness, but lacks the Kural's stress on speaking kindly to everyone without exception and on escaping poverty; Bhai Gurdas is exegesis, not scripture.

95.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
95.explanation: In the Asa di Vaar, after describing the showy but fruitless simmal tree, Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility as the very core of all good qualities.
95.tie_back: It is nearly the Kural's own verdict: humility and sweet speech are a person's true ornament, and nothing else deserves the name.
95.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
95._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one pairing of humility and sweetness as the highest good; Gurbani calls them the essence of virtue rather than using the Kural's image of ornament.

96.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger. Your body shall not suffer from any disease, and you shall obtain everything.”
96.explanation: Sheikh Farid counsels returning good for evil without harbouring anger, promising wholeness and every good thing as the result.
96.tie_back: As the Kural says good words sought out and kindly spoken make evil wane and virtue grow, Farid holds that answering evil with good overcomes it.
96.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 78) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
96._accuracy_note: Good fit on goodness diminishing evil, but Farid speaks of good deeds in general, not specifically of carefully chosen, pleasant speech.

97.quote_or_event: “By speaking sweetly, behaving humbly and bestowing charities with one's own hands, even the fallen ones have become pure.”
97.explanation: Bhai Gurdas teaches that sweet speech joined to humble conduct and giving is so powerful that it can redeem even those who had fallen.
97.tie_back: Like the Kural's speech that never strays from good character and so brings both goodwill and merit, Bhai Gurdas ties sweet words to conduct and credits them with moral transformation.
97.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 29, Pauri 4 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)
97._accuracy_note: Partial: shares speech-bound-to-character and its moral fruit, but not the Kural's twin reward of social goodwill; Bhai Gurdas is exegesis, not scripture.

98.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid. He is called the most insipid of the insipid; the most insipid of the insipid is his reputation. The insipid person is discarded in the Court of the Lord, and the insipid one's face is spat upon.”
98.explanation: Guru Nanak warns that harsh, graceless speech sours the speaker inwardly, ruins his name among people and leaves him rejected in God's court.
98.tie_back: It states the Kural's promise in reverse: kind words free of meanness bring joy in this life and the next, while their opposite brings disgrace in both.
98.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
98._accuracy_note: Strong mirror-image fit covering both this world (reputation) and the next (the Lord's Court), though framed as a warning rather than as the Kural's positive promise.

99.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor. Harsh words bring only grief. Listen, O foolish and ignorant mind!”
99.explanation: Guru Nanak contrasts words that bring honour with harsh words that bring only grief, and calls the mind that still chooses harshness foolish.
99.tie_back: Like Valluvar's puzzled question, it treats harsh speech as plain folly in one who knows how much good kind words do.
99.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
99._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the sweet/harsh contrast and the folly of harshness; it lacks the Kural's appeal to the speaker's own experience of being spoken to kindly.

100.quote_or_event: “He thinks that the ripe coconut hangs on the barren simmal tree; what a stupid, idiotic fool he is!”
100.explanation: In a Raamkalee hymn Kabir mocks the deluded person who mistakes worthless fruit for good and turns from what would truly nourish him.
100.tie_back: Like Valluvar's man who grabs unripe fruit while the ripe hangs beside it, Kabir's fool chooses the barren over the good through sheer perversity.
100.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 972, Raag Raamkalee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
100._accuracy_note: Close on the fruit image and the folly of choosing badly, but Kabir's subject is spiritual delusion in general, not harsh versus pleasant speech.
